utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning, Mr. Puhovski. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Misetic will now continue his you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Professor.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would like to start off with a topic and show you a video first to address another issue for which you may have some knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The video, Mr. Registrar, is 1D67-0211.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And professor you will notice this is a television interview that you gave to the Croatian state television programme, Sundays at 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] "Stankovic: Now that you have mentioned this Veritas, for many Croatian it is an enigma. What is Veritas. "Zarko Puhovski: Basically Veritas is a non-governmental organisation in Serbia led by former functionaries of what was once called the Republic of Serbian Krajina as well as some younger individuals that have joined as well. The ambition of Veritas is to provide a complex overview of all the Serb victims in the wars from 1991 to 1995, that is that they have even expanded this further on to 1999 in Kosovo, et cetera, to the bombing, and furthermore, according to its own opinion, it provides objective facts regarding these victims. On a number of occasions when faced with their findings, we determined that parts of these findings were incorrect. And unfortunately, part of these incorrect findings influenced the Prosecution in of The Hague Tribunal for reasons that I'm not able to comment upon, as I simply don't know them. Not in order to be secretive here but because I don't know why this came to be, why they did this. We warned those who wished to listen to us when they wished to listen. They would always listen to us politely and then proceed according to their wishes. Let me return to what I was saying earlier. When we talk about surprises, I'm not saying that I was looking over Ms. Del Ponte's shoulder, but I think they possess certain information that they did not use, and it seems unbelievable to me that they wouldn't use these facts. The Defence has information as well. The issue, of course, is to what extent will the Defence be able to sufficiently organise itself? Will it have enough time? And will it, I would dare say, fall into the pressure that is being exerted to join the Gotovina, Cermak, Markac cases together, or will it see that it would perhaps be better to separate these cases?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor, on that video it seems that you have some reservations it Veritas. And I wanted to just seek your comments as to whether you indeed have reservations about them and what the basis of your reservations are.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reservations, and this is something that the Helsinki Committee referred to in two of its statements, therefore, is not my reservations alone. Has to do with three elements. First the morale integrity aspect. The leaders of Veritas like Savo Strbac were proponents of a regime which in our view constituted a denial of human rights. Secondly, because the organisation had dealt with a very selective process. In other words it selected the victims along ethnic lines. Of course, it is important to determine how many victims there were on individual sides, but there has to be an objective approach. Thirdly, we were sometimes in a situation where our colleagues in the field were able to ascertain that the data they had published was simply not true. In some of our statements, made by, for instance, colleague Hellebrandt and colleague Gazivoda, we went public with this in 2002, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the video be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1322, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1322 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have on the screen now 1D67-0365.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, you recall from yesterday that I asked you to keep in mind one of the names that -- two of the names that Mr. Pilsel had given to the Office of the Prosecutor, Carlos Zvonimir. And I'd like to show you a document of the Croatian police at the moment. Now, this is a police -- this is an Official Note, and in it you will see that according to the police, in the second paragraph there was a vehicle. In the proximity of the vehicle several persons were present, officers of the crime politician approached the same in order to establish the reason of their stay in the settlement Komic because nobody is currently residing there. And it says: "At the site the persons were identified as ..." There are individuals listed. Number three, the person present is Carlos Zvonimir, born in Buenos Aires, Argentina, vice president of the Croatian Helsinki committee. Number 4 is Jadranko Mrkalj who is, I believe you indicated, the son of Petar Mrkalj. If you go down to the bottom after the last name, it says the above mentioned Magdic, Mario and Ozegovic Hasim were found putting post-mortem remains of decomposed bodies in a wooden casket, and the officers of the crime police department conducted informative interviews with all of the mentioned persons regarding ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... the circumstances of the discovery of the dead bodies, at which point it was established that the bodies were identified by the citizen Momcilovic Dusanka as the following persons. And then identifies the deceased. And then it says: "The above mentioned citizens intended to conduct burial of the bodies at the Komic local cemetery even though they had not previously informed the competent organs and the chief of the crime police department of Zadar-Knin police administration, Mr. Ive Kardum was immediately notified of the events who then notified the public prosecutor and the investigating judge in Zadar, and the above mentioned persons were prohibited from burying the bodies until the arrival of the on-site investigation team." You can turn the page in Croatian, please, but ... Now my question, Professor, is why wouldn't members of the Helsinki Committee upon the discovery of a body report this to the appropriate authorities for processing, and do you have any knowledge of this incident and why the Croatian Helsinki Committee would start to bury remains rather than contact the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to repeat. At least on 30 occasions, between the summer of 1995, and unless I'm mistaken this is early 1996, we turned to various local authorities, in particular the Zadar police administration. We had never met up with any response. In this particular instance, the dead bodies were deposing. Mr. Jovan Nikolic, the Orthodox priest was summoned, and I believe he was the only Orthodox priest active in Croatia at the time. So that in line with the custom and religious tradition, the individuals had -- the remains of the individuals who had for at least three weeks been lying exposed be buried, and this is something the neighbours were aware of, as well as the members of the local authorities. Nobody did anything. We believed it was our task to do something about it. As soon as our representatives appeared, of course, the police force emerged, and seemingly wanted to show that it was very active.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the statement it says at the top of page 2, which is in the middle of the English translation there, that Momcilovic Dusanka in the course of the interview, it was established that the same discovered the bodies on 15 February 1996, but didn't report the same to anyone except the Helsinki Committee in Karlovac. Do you know if the Helsinki committee between the time it was reported to the Helsinki committee and the time they intended to do the burial that they contacted the Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I don't know, but I do not believe that they did. It is quite telling that the lady believed that the Helsinki Committee is the one she needs to turn to rather than the local police authorities which only goes to show what sort of a reputation they enjoyed among the citizens in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1323, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1323 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I would like to turn your attention now to a different portion of the Helsinki Committee report which is page 82 in the English. I'll try to find it in the Croatian, the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Registrar, this is exhibit 65 ter 4674. In the Croatian it's page 81 in e-court; page 80 in the original. Okay. Sorry, it's the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, I can show you first here, and then we'll go back to that previous page in English. But you have the original in front of you, Professor. What I'm interested in is the number of burned houses. You quote General Forand as having stated on the 10th of October, 1995, that according to his data, the UN military observers visited 320 villages and counted 22.000 burned houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go back one page in the English, please, which is again back one page in the Croatian version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's that paragraph which is the third paragraph. It says: "In the former UN Sector South at least 22.000 houses and a number of villages were burned in a systematic and organised manner." Now the report seems to cite General Forand on the 10th of October for the number that is 22.000 burned houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could pull up Exhibit P400, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, the number of 22.000 burned houses is a number that was then used in the film, Storm over Krajina as the number of burned houses. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this is, Professor, the press statement of General Forand on the 12th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the fourth paragraph, if we can go to page 2 in the Croatian, yes. Fourth paragraph. The first thing I would to -- let's just talk about the number 22.000. What General Forand seems to have said is that 21.744 houses were observed over 16.578 were destroyed by fire or severely damaged. Before you give your answer, I can tell you I will explore with you the number of 16.578 in a minute. But just do you see that in fact the number of 22.000 is General Forand's number of houses observed and not houses burned or destroyed, as is indicated in the HHO report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, so -- now we get to the number of 16.578 destroyed by fire or severely damaged. And I would just like to show you a few samples of the methodology and analysis that went into that number. And you may have actually some knowledge, given your knowledge of this area, that you may be able to help us out to understand some of the complexities here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have on the screen 1D67-0265, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now what I'm going to you show you step by step this is, for example, an analysis of the number of burned homes in the Korenica area. And can you see what we've done is we've put Korenica, which is in the middle towards the bottom middle, is the city of Korenica, as well as all of the outlying villages in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We've -- what we did was then we went to the official census of the Republic of Croatia, 1991 to talk about the total number of inhabitants in the entire wider Korenica area of Serbs and Croats as well as the total number of dwellings in that wider area, so they're all plotted in terms of the numbers. It is clear that the Serbs were the overwhelming majority in the Korenica area and the total buildings according to the census is 947.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now just a breakdown of the number of buildings in each of the cities, villages -- city, villages, and hamlets. We've broken it down. It's the population as well as the total buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is again a continuation of the remaining four hamlets which gives the ethnic composition as well as the total buildings according to the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And now if we go to the final page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First let me ask you, just in fairness to you, Professor, are you able to understand this in English, or would you like to us put a --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a break down now. And the UNMO analysis of the number of burned buildings in Korenica, they only included three of the eight villages and hamlets in Korenica municipality. We went ahead and assumed that perhaps the UNMOs didn't know that these were separate areas, so we included them just in case they didn't separate it out. So if you look at the total viewed according UNMO, if you go to the column that says total viewed, according to the UNMO report, they viewed 3215 houses. And then it says how many were totally destroyed and partially destroyed. You see that they say 622 were total destroyed. 2.953 were partially destroyed. Now if you go to the column that says the total number the buildings in 1991, you will see that where the UNMO said that they viewed 3.000 buildings in Korenica, there were only 617 in Korenica according to the census. In Seganovac they viewed 15; there were 26. In Vrelo Korenicko there were 200 that UNMO says it viewed, but there were only 90 on the census. And if you go down and add them all up, and then we went ahead and proceeded to include in numbers 4 through 8 any other villages in that area that may have mistakenly been included as part of Titova Korenica, and you get a total of 947 total buildings according to the census. And I can just tell you, in case there's any confusion, that earlier on in this case there was testimony by Mr. Anttila and under questioning by Judge Gwaunza. This is at page 2.673 beginning at line 24, going over to the next page, and ending at line 12. Judge Gwaunza asked maybe -- and I will read it out. She says: "Can I ask you, would you know whether in giving those figures they would include, for instance, the number of buildings or structures that may have been burning or that may have been burnt within one homestead. In other words I'm asking if a team visit the one homestead where there is a house in other smaller structures outside, and they found that the house and the structures were burning. In their reports would they say five structures were burning, or would they say one, referring to the homestead?" And Mr. Antilla responded: "To my understanding the teams considered houses as houses where people would be living, so they would not be considering sheds for the livestock and so on. That was their task anyway." Now this is the example of Korenica. Do you see that the number of 16.000 that General Forand mentions, in fact, there is an significant variance now when we look at Korenica between the total number of houses they claim to have viewed and the total number of buildings that actually were recorded in the 1991 census. Professor?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the possibility that that number of 16.000 may be inflated?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three sources we drew upon. One was the United Nations, or their observers, in other words; the second one was the official position of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Mr. Granic, who said that 5.000 homes destroyed during combat alone, and we found a great many that were destroyed later on. And in addition to that, we used our findings from various areas to draw inferences. Because we had limited resources, human and materiel resources, we weren't able to go out into each and every area, but on the basis of the observation made with regard to certain localities, we drew inferences which were consistent with these ones here. Our first findings that were presented as an approximation in the HHO report were -- had to do roughly with 20.000 homes from both sectors. And this figure was later on used by the UN sources and by various NGOs and the press. I repeat, again, these were inferences that we made on the basis of the findings from the areas observed. As far as this discrepancy is concerned, let me draw your attention to one possibility that we entertained as well. Here in fact the case was that the former Yugoslav municipalities which were much larger, were confused with the new system of the Republic of Croatia where the municipalities were far smaller. And at times we would have a great confusion like in the area of Kostajnica and Korenica. And this is just an offhand theory now that I'm drawing your attention to as a possible explanation. As far as the methodology used by foreign observers and how they might have arrived at the figures they have arrived at, that is something that I cannot comment upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, first let me just clarify. HHO didn't do its own systematic assessment of the number of burned buildings. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those reports you have that, in several dozens of communities we counted those houses. Other results are extrapolated from other reports, so they are not a fruit of systematic research.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that the actual report, the HHO report from 2001, doesn't cite any statement by Minister Granic in support of the number. What it does is rely on General Forand's assessment in terms of what is explicitly in the report.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I would like to take a look at a different municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1324, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can also tell you we have submitted the underlying census and information to the Prosecution. If the Court wishes that we mark those and tender those for the benefit of the Court, we're capable of doing that as well. It's up to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll give it some thought, whether we will invite to you tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could now have 1D67-0275.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the village of Licki Osik and the surrounding area. What we have done is we've put a map together with the confrontation line as of the 3rd of August. And we can see that Licki Osik is in fact a front line village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now, we have put in again the wider villages and hamlets that were on both sides of the confrontation line as well as the ethnic breakdown. And you can see that there's a roughly equivalent ethnic breakdown of the Licki Osik and surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now a further breakdown in detail of the various villages and hamlets that make up Licki Osik, and can you tell, for example, Licki Osik itself is a roughly ethnically balanced area, as is Siroka Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again we have done the same type of analysis, comparing what UNMO says were the total number of viewed buildings, comparing it to the number of buildings that actually existed in 1991, and you can see -- you can see that there's a difference. What I'm particularly interested in, though, is if we look at Licki Osik and we assume for the sake of argument that every building, meaning of the 953 that were there in 1991, if we assume for the sake of argument that every building there was completely or partly damaged, given the ethnic composition there, meaning 1570 Serbs, against -- I shouldn't say against - with 1156 Croats, can you explain why or what the circumstances would be that might lead to the complete destruction of a village that has a rough ethnic balance?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, Licki Osik was not completely destroyed. Almost two thirds of edifices remained undamaged. Don't hold me to the percentage, but roughly, that's first. Secondly, we have seen situations where mixed population villages completely destroyed. First one side would destroy the other side's houses, and then the other side would destroy the first side's houses. But I'm not sure that I know that this happened in Licki Osik. And I reiterate it is not known to me that Licki Osik has been destroyed to that extent as some other communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Based on your answer, I have two questions. One, then if in fact two thirds it wasn't destroyed, then that would mean that the UNMOs numbers with respect to Licki Osik would be significantly less than what they reported, correct, because they reported 800 --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So that's the first point. The second point is you have now mentioned something that in fact is probably true which is that areas that were under Serb control that were of mixed ethnicity in 1993, let's say, could have had Croat houses damaged or destroyed, and then in 1995 people who returned to that village did the same to the Serb houses. My question is when you then try to do an assessment of the entire area, and you come up with numbers like this for houses totally or partly destroyed it's very difficult then to determine who did the destroying, how many of the houses were destroyed prior to August 1995, how many were destroyed subsequently. Certainly if you are at the UNMO. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our colleagues who went out on the ground, they cynically called humane botany, you would see in houses that had been destroyed for two or three years, you could find vegetation, even trees growing out of such ruins. And it was very accurate, although primitive, criterion to tell those two types of damaged houses apart. There were houses where trees were growing out of -- so that they could have been destroyed in the summer that we investigated that situation. We took that into account. It would -- it was very easy to tell those apart. Very few houses were destroyed by the Serbs in the summer of 1995. Most of the buildings that were destroyed were destroyed when the Serbs had recently taken control of the area, as it was in 1991 and beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You, however, don't know whether the internationals when they were doing this, how accurate they were in distinguishing pre-Operation Storm and post-Operation Storm damage; correct? You didn't review their work.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not check, but when you read their reports it is obvious that they hadn't done that, whenever they did so, they listed or enumerated buildings and recorded buildings that were useable and damaged -- and buildings that had been damaged. They evidenced the degree of destruction and maybe the cause, whether it was fighting or some other cause of destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1325, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, I'd like to take you now to Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which, Mr. Registrar, is 1D67-0294.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the village of Kistanje with all of its surrounding hamlets, and, once again, what we've done is we have included every hamlet and village in the Kistanje area and put the census material together. So you see the number of the Serbs versus the number of Croats there in 1991. And according to the census how many total buildings there were in the entire wider Kistanje area, and it's 547 buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now we have taken then the UNMO report from November of 1995 and put all -- anything that is from the Kistanje municipality on the chart, and put their assessments of total viewed, completely damaged, and partly damaged. And according to their report, which is Exhibit P176 in evidence, there were 101 completely damaged buildings in Kistanje and 63 partly damaged. Now, not to minimise the amount of damage, which is not my intention, but what I wish to point out, though, is compared to the census figures, it would indicate that there is roughly one third of the buildings in Kistanje were either completely or partly damaged when compared to the census figures of 1991, according to UNMO. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the damage to Kistanje, this number now, that comes to again roughly one third, or to be precise, 164 completely or partly damaged buildings out of 547. That number, 164, is from a report dated November of -- November 4, 1995. You're familiar with the fact that Kistanje wasn't -- that the damage in Kistanje didn't occur at one instance; it was -- it continued to pop up for several weeks after Operation Storm. There would be other incidents of burning. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It is stated on page 93 of our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1326, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D12 -- just one second, what's the number. D1326 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then one last assessment on this issue, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is 1D67-0373 please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What we did was, Professor, we took nine municipalities from the UNMO assessment. This is just nine. There are more. We didn't have time to go through all of it. But if you -- we start to flip through. You can read across, we took the UNMO assessment and put them in the proper municipalities. So, for example, you can look at the Benkovac municipality which is the first municipality there. Then you can look at various villages that are referenced in the UNMO report from the Benkovac municipality. We gave -- we put in the number of buildings in those villages in 1991, compared it with the UNMO assessment of total viewed, completely damaged, and partly damaged, provided you with an assessment of the ethnic composition of those areas, and then we have a column that says the difference and identify the UNMO team involved. You can -- we can with scroll down. For example, we did the same for Drnis, Donji Lapac, Gospic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's Knin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have the B/C/S version on our screen at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that we can have the English version. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Knin and -- it is referred to as Titova Korenica because that was the name prior to 1991. It is now just Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Otocac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Senj and Sibenik. And now there's the total line at the building. You can see that the total number of buildings in this municipalities -- at least I should say the villages, cities, and hamlets referenced in the UNMO report within these municipalities. The total number of buildings in 1991 was 6342, but UNMO claimed to have viewed 13851 in that area and claimed to have found 10647 completely or partly damaged buildings in those areas. And if you compare the total viewed against the total number of buildings that were documented in 1991, that's a difference of 7500 buildings. If you take the total number of damaged buildings alleged to have been found, which is 10647, and subtract out the total number of buildings that actually there were in 1991, the difference is 4305 more buildings than UNMO claims to have -- had been completely or partly damaged than the 1991 census recognises as having even existed at that time. And that assumes that every buildings that existed in 1991 was partly or totally damaged. My point, Professor, is that this number that has been bandied about over the course of the years of 22.000 burned houses, very much relies on the assessment of the UNMOs, which you will concede, you have never actually sat down, looked at that report and tried to do a scholarly analysis after that report that you might do at Zagreb university, for example. There is no scholarly assessment that you have attempted to do of that assessment.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just three things. On page 93 that I cited just a minute ago in our report, it is clearly stated that we did not count damage and burned houses, that these were assessment. Another thing, any sociologist would say this to you, the Yugoslav census was based on the concept of household. It's a patriarchical concept, so there are certain edifices which are connected with every household. The UNMOs must have counted barns and some other outbuildings, and this is the only way that they could have come up with such a number. So you didn't take into account just the main building but also the pigsty or cowshed and sheds for other types of cattle. So they must have counted each of them separately, and this is the only explanation that seems to me plausible. Although there is this possibility, that somebody, you know, just invented those numbers, but it doesn't seem true to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, there is also the possibility that this assessment was done in a moving vehicle, driving down the main roads, and just by eyesight trying to make estimates of how many buildings are in the village, how many were destroyed, et cetera. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to, because this is something that I cannot discount. But the situation was too serious, and it still is, to let somebody just drive around or approach the same place down two different roads and then count double. I would like to believe that this is a difference in methodology and not a job lacking seriousness. But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a factual question. Did the HHO have the underlying UNMO assessment when it was preparing this report? Meaning -- let me be specific. I don't mean just a report of a number. I mean did you have the UNMO report, village by village, hamlet by hamlet, of the counting they were doing?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1327, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1327, I heard, is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Two short topic areas, Mr. President, and I will be finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor, let me show you - if I can find it - 1D67-0099, please. I want to show you two exhibits to save some time, Professor, so first I will show you this one, I'll show you the next one. This is an article from Nacional from 15 October 1997. It is an interview given by Cedo Prodanovic who at the time was a member of the Presidency of the Croatian Helsinki Committee. You can see in the picture, and again this is it October 1997, there's a picture there, and it is Mr. Prodanovic and Mr. Cicak standing in front of the Tribunal. And this is his interview discussing a meeting that was held between Mr. Prodanovic and Mr. Cicak on the one side with the Office of the Prosecutor. And I'd like to just point out a few comments of Mr. Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go -- in the Croatian we will have to blow this up because the print is very small. It's at the bottom far left-hand column. There we go. And in the English it starts at the bottom of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "The first question regarded the reasons for which he and Ivan Zvonimir Cicak travelled to The Hague." And Mr. Prodanovic said: "Mr. Cicak and I went to The Hague upon the invitation of the OTP of the international Tribunal as officials of the Croatian Helsinki Committee which is part of an international organisation for the protection of human rights. The ICTY demonstrated" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... an interest for the activities of the HHO, so they invited us to give them firsthand information regarding our work." And a few sentences down. It says: "A great deal of data collect in the field by our activists was interesting to the international Tribunal in The Hague. Therefore, we mainly discussed determining the methodology of our work so that our collaboration would be as effective as possible." Now, actually let me ask you a few questions while we have this here. Are you aware of the circumstances of this visit of Mr. Prodanovic and Mr. Cicak to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was talk about that at the executive committee after they had returned. They reported briefly to their colleagues on their stay in The Hague. I was still in the Helsinki Committee at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prodanovic says, "They invited us to give them firsthand information regarding our work," and then he goes on to say, "We mainly discussed determining the methodology of our work so that our collaboration would be as effective as possible." What was the methodology that was agreed upon between the HHO and Mr. Prodanovic, on the one hand, and the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, we informed the people in The Hague about our methodology. They were only launching their investigation and were interested in knowing how this was done in the region. We acquainted them with our methodology. By that time the material for the report had already been finished, and we were contemplating its distribution by way of photocopies. To my knowledge, this had to do with us conveying to them our experience in relation to the investigations done into the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1328.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I'd now like to show a video. This is 1D67-0209, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] "Stankovic: What does this mean? Are there aggravating or mitigating circumstances for Gotovina, and how do you know this? "Zarko Puhovski: I don't know this. I can't say that I know what they know, but I do know that there are some additional facts which they received which weren't in the indictment, some of which are positive, some negative. "Stankovic: Which type of facts do you think prevail? "Zarko Puhovski: In my opinion with regards to the current indictment, there are more positive than negative facts. "Stankovic: You are not able to comment further? "Zarko Puhovski: I cannot say anything because these are clearly matters of an internal nature. They know them. Now whether or not they will use them is a different issue. "Stankovic: Does this mean that the HHO participated in disclosing these documents? "Zarko Puhovski: We gave them everything we had to the state attorney, the police, and representatives of the court in The Hague. What a what they did with these materials is partly evident now. Unfortunately, they used other sources as well, namely, Veritas and others, which we discussed, if you recall, almost five years ago in your show. There was nothing we could do about this whatsoever."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm interested in the last comment where you say that, "We gave everything we had to the state attorney, the police, and the representatives of the Court in The Hague. What they did with these materials is partly evident now." My question is a combination of your statement on this TV programme and Mr. Prodanovic's talk about a methodology. The underlying reports the investigations in the field, the notes, the data on the computer database, you seem to indicate, and that's why I'm asking to correct me now, that this material was given to the proper authorities. Mr. Prodanovic is in The Hague in 1997 discussing the methodology of cooperation between OTP and the HHO. Why weren't the underlying reports submitted to the Office of the Prosecutor at least, so that we could verify some of the witness statements that are referred to in this report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, we handed over our reports when they were finished in 1999 -- or, rather, we sent them to some 300 addresses. I have already mentioned this. From the office of the president to all the state agencies, to all the embassies, to the Zagreb office of the ICTY. This is what we did with the material at the time. At times, members of certain Defence teams approached us for information and at the time when I was president of the HHO we provided the information to everyone who asked for it. In other words we did not adopt specific approach depending on who turned to us. We provided whatever material we could gather at the time, in the premises of the HHO. It all revolved, in essence, around the report that is being analysed here, and that was available to everyone. I don't know that anything changed in the work methodology. Once Mr. Prodanovic and Mr. Cicak returned from The Hague. I don't think this had to do with anything beyond that which they said here. In other words that they discussed the way that we went about things and the way we were still going about things at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand that the report was circulated. But as you probably are aware, Ms. Higgins asked you, and I'm asking you, the underlying information that forms the report, you indicated that Mr. Mrkalj, Jadranko Mrkalj has that information and was asking money for it. I'm asking you why that underlying information, instead of going to Mr. Jadranko Mrkalj, didn't get sent to the Office of the Prosecutor for their use or, alternatively, to the Croatian state prosecutor's office or the Croatian state police?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the reasons I mentioned the other day, all the data was in the possession of Petar Mrkalj. Upon his death they were in possession of his son. None of us sought the material, though we would have liked to have our copies of the material, we did not believe it necessary to pay for it. The material was held in private hands because Mr. Petar Mrkalj lived in fear of the control of the military secret service over the HHO, and that's why he kept all the material in his own apartment in Karlovac, and that's why they stayed with his son ultimately, and his fears proved to be true in fact. Nobody asked me personally to give the underlying material in relation to the report, and I, myself, wanted to have my own archive of it and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the interpreter please finish.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I wanted to have an archive of my own, but I did not ultimately have it, due to the fact that I didn't want to pay for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think there is an error in English transcript, page 26 line 11, where it says "none of us sought the material." I think the witness might have said something different in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will verify that. When you said upon his death they were in possession of his son, referring to this materials, and then in the next line you said, it starts in the transcript, "none of us," and then the part that follows, Ms. Frolich has raised some doubts, and then the end of that sentence is, "although we would have liked to have copies of the material." Could you tell us what did you say about seeking the material, did you, did you not, did none of you? Did it ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The material concerned consisted of handwritten notes made on the basis of the field work and audiotapes, all of which were used for the drafting of the report. The material was in the apartment belong to Petar Mrkalj in Karlovac at the time when he died. He kept them there because he was afraid that somebody would steel them from the HHO office. When he died, his son, Jadranko Mrkalj inherited them. I tried to obtain the material from Jadranko Mrkalj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so where the transcript reads, "none of us sought the material," is that inaccurate? Because that's what we read on our transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Nobody ever asked us to hand over the material underlying the report. I, as the president, asked to have the material because I wanted to have a complete archive. However, I, as a president, or any of my colleagues were never asked by anyone to provide the underlying material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, because I'm getting a bit confused, finally, Jadranko Mrkalj asked money for it. And finally did you obtain that material, or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. We decided that we would not be paying in exchange for the material, and, consequently, we did not obtain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So, therefore, it was not in your possession so as to provide it to anyone. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. They were not, and no -- nobody asked us to provide them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask that the video be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1329 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Last document, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could 1D67-0249, please. Can we scroll to the top of the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor, this seems to be a fax line from you at the top with a date and a time stamp. And it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is titled to the Croatian Helsinki Committee for human rights members, dated 17 May 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please, just to look at the signature. There is a signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor, this is your resignation letter to the Croatian Helsinki Committee in 1998. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn back in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you in fact resigned from the Helsinki Committee in 1998, and you provided the committee with your reasoning for why you were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the bottom paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Amongst other things, you write that for a longer period, the committee was too often (because sometimes it is almost inevitable) and uncritically involved into the party and political activities, and, respectively, it was tendentiously reduced to the media promotion apparatus." First, can you explain what types of things was the committee doing at the time which led you to conclude that the committee was uncritically involved into the party and political activities?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several members of the committee, contrary to the logic of an NGO, were involved in the activities of certain political parties, or supported them, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which members of the committee were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several individuals. For instance, Mr. Cicak, who participated in several political party activities, although not as a member of the party. Like, for instance, those of the HSLS. And I was referring to Mr. Banac. Primarily I was referring to the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You continue on that that paragraph, and you say: "Lately, perhaps, it seemed that racing sponsors on the basis of, according to me, misunderstood professionalism, pushed aside the original mandate of the HHO. The HHO has dealt more and more with what foreign donators requested, e.g., war crimes, for which I am convinced it is, in principle, questionable whether they are within the scope of our work." Can you comment on what exactly you meant there that the HHO was dealing more with what foreign donators requested. What foreign donators are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, the spring of 1998, we had around 30 employees, and it required smooth working. Unlike the initial small organisation, as it grew in number, it became less flexible. The donors concerned were the Soros Foundation, primarily the Soros Foundation at the time. The Helsinki Committees from Sweden, and Norway, Denmark, and the Netherlands, as well as the USAID, the USAID organisation. At the time more than half of the funds were donated by the Soros Foundation. That was roughly the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you believe that these foreign donors were focussing the work of the HHO on war crimes, and why did you believe that it was questionable whether this was within the scope of the HHO's work?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed to me that, regardless of the large number of employees, our resources were quite limited, and our main task was to be concerned with the violation of the rights of the living. I believe that the bulk of our work on the other issue had been done in 1995 and 1996. A month or two before this, I suggested that the special department concerned with war crimes within the HHO and which had four to five employees, should discontinue its activity. I felt that we no longer needed it with the lapse of time. This was the part that was in dispute. It was felt by some others that we could attract a lot of funds from donors if we pursued this activity. I'm telling you that this is happening some three years after the end of the war, and my feeling was that there was no need to be involved in this specifically. Rather, that we should concentrate on the people turning to our office, seeking for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor, that's actually the point I wanted to get to. You left in 1998 before the first report came out in 1999. Do you agree with me that the report in 1999 was written, trying to put as much -- as much -- as many allegations as possible in the report to justify the foreign financing that had gone into the HHO, and that may be one of the reasons why the underlying documentation that supports the report is in fact missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to object. This calls for a speculative answer on the part of the witness who was not present in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know. But the question could be put in such a way that whatever fear you may have on whether it calls for speculation could be taken away. Mr. Misetic, I leave it in your hands how to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor, you're one of the founders of the HHO. You have spent many years in that organisation. You resigned as a result of some of the issues that you have mentioned in the letter, including the fact that -- I think you have just testified that some people in the organisation felt that dealing with war crimes was a good way to get money for the organisation and that you resigned out of principle for that reason. My question to you is: Do you agree with me that it is entirely possible that 1999 report was compiled to justify the foreign financing that had gone into the HHO, but the underlying documentation has never surfaced so that the report itself can never be verified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I left it in your hands. But these are two questions, as a matter of fact. And what you're doing at this moment is, we should clearly distinguish between several issues apparently here. Mr. Puhovski, you said you thought that no attention was needed anymore for war crimes, but apparently foreign sponsors were pushing for war crime activities. Is that how I understand -- I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't say that they exerted pressure. A decision had to be made to stop receiving certain funds, which the committee was in dire need of. So it was that sort of pressure, financial pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. But -- and some of you thought that continuation of paying attention to war crimes would favour further funding by these foreign sponsors. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat, unless I'm mistaken, we had a three-year contract. My suggestion was that we should terminate the contract, because I believed that we had done everything that was in our power. This would mean that the cash-flow would stop. The idea was not that we would be receiving these funds beyond 2000. Rather, we were under the contract, supposed to receive the funds until the end of 1999, whereas my suggestion was that we should stop it -- that we should terminate the contract with the beginning of 1998 and close down the department that dealt with these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further attention for war crimes and ending a contract which would fund such activities. That was your position. Now, finally, do I understand that this funding continued and that that department paying attention to war crimes continue its activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the end of 1999, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Misetic did put a question to you in which he implied, more or less, that paying further attention to war crimes would also mean that you would have the maximum number of allegations on war crimes. Now, paying attention to investigating war crimes and getting the highest number of war crimes is -- is not exactly the same. If -- did you ever feel any pressure to focus on investigation of war crimes; or did you also feel, perhaps, pressure to produce as many war crimes as possible, or allegations of war crimes? Was it just the subject, or was it also the result, the outcome of such investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a very long conversation about this in 1996 with Mr. Ari Neiyer [phoen] who was in charge of that field of work of the Soros Foundation which was our main sponsor. Mr. Neiyer is one of the world renowned experts for the investigation of war crimes and violations of human rights. When he came to see our team again in 1997, he kept alerting us to the fact that we should rather leave out some of the allegations rather than publish them and be proved wrong. In his capacity as a donor, he insisted on us being very careful with figures, and it seemed a reasonable position to me. The pressure, the financial pressure, that is, was on the topic itself and not on the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps there is one element in your question which has not been answered yet, and perhaps you put it to the witness, that is about whether the underlying documentation was kept away in order to -- I leave that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I can follow up on that question first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor, that is what happened in 1996. However, with respect to what happened after you left, and your resignation letter talks and you've testified now about Mr. Cicak engaging in certain political activities. But my question is this: You understand that there were hundreds of thousands of dollars that were put into the HHO by these foreign donors. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At a certain point in time, we received some 500.000 dollars a year, let's say in 1997, 1998, the amount was worth much more than it is it today. Let me just, for the sake of illustration, tell that you in 1998, my professorial salary was some 500 dollars, which is more than four times lower than today, so we could say that the difference was -- difference was four-fold.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... actually, you say that in your resignation letter. You make reference to the fact that you're the only activist in the HHO, everybody else was paid against professional, social, or commercial logic? My point to you is that people who were getting paid as professionals or under commercial logic within the HHO, you have to produce results for people that are putting 500.000 dollars a year into your organisation, right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without any doubt. It says 3.500.000 in the record. That is error. 500.000 is what I referred to. You see the HHO had its finances secured on a basis of a long-term plan. We had been given funds and the Soros Foundation was satisfied with the outcome of our activities. There was no need for us to produce something in order to satisfy anybody. The only insistence was that we should continue our investigations into the war crimes which was something that I felt was pointless. But nobody asked directly or indirectly that we adjust in any way, increase or expand the results for such-and-such a purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Two short questions because we're coming up on a break, and I would like to finish before the break. First, was it understood, was it not, that as a result of this financing there had to be some final report by the HHO. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Second, you have talked about Mr. Mrkalj was afraid of the Croatian intelligence services and therefore hid the underlying information at home. My question is posing an alternative, which is that Mr. Mrkalj kept the underlying information not only outside the HHO but never gave it to the Office of the Prosecutor, to Croatian prosecutors, or the Croatian police, because he knew that the report, in 1999, didn't have supporting underlying documentation for all of the allegations in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Again, this is calling for speculation on what Mrkalj' motives might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we could ask Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could make a response. She's put into evidence on direct what Mrkalj was afraid of the intelligence services, so if that's speculation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I understood that to be that -- what we should ask the witness is whether Mr. Mrkalj told him any such thing or whether there is in the fact to his knowledge, which would be in line or not in line with either the one or the other explanation. That is -- we'll ask the witness for facts, and I leave it in your hands, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The Judge is asking for facts, Professor, but my question is also tied to your experience in the HHO. Your knowledge, intimate knowledge of the internal workings of that organisation. First, did Mr. Mrkalj tell you explicitly that he didn't want the underlying information to come to light because it might undermine the credibility of the report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkalj spoke to me and others on the committee on several occasions, and he even wrote letters about being afraid of the military service. This is no secret, and these are facts that can be corroborated by the HHO archive. He never told me anything of the sort. When I said the -- when the report was published, not a single objection was made to it, save for that one, which as I said, we managed to prove the objection was wrong. When the report was published in photocopies in 1999 and when it was published as a book in 2001, we had reason to believe that everything contained in it was corroborated. What was clear to me was that the associates working for Mr. Mrkalj wrote information on their own. So they knew that there was underlying documentation. I spent hours upon hours listening to the audiotapes of the interviews made in the field. I was listening to the people working in the field, reading their notes and I was aware of their existence at the time. Unfortunately, I don't know where the material is today. I can testify that in 1995, 1996, and 1997, the material did exist. I cannot vouch for the entire report, of course, but I can vouch for the parts of it for which I did the debriefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Professor Puhovski, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit on the screen be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1330, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1330 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, pursuant to what I said on the record yesterday, we have put together a bar table submission for the remaining documents concerning Mr. Puhovski's testimony. It has been submitted to the OTP, and I'm advised that OTP has no objection. I could be wrong, obviously but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: If I could have until after the break to just verify that once again. Thank you very much. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you were so kind to offer the underlying census material to add to the material. The Chamber would appreciate if could you add that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That will in our bar table then as well, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Puhovski, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Since we're speaking the same language, I would like to ask you to pause between my question and your answer, so that the interpreters may do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, during your testimony, you were asked and discussed the methodology whereby the HHO activists collected information and data. You also said that you -- HHO activists verified data by returning to the same place where they got the data from to verify what they were told. At the time, was it possible to obtain official data from the police, the competent state prosecutor or judiciary, at large?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my experience, it -- the top of the police structure, Minister Jarnjak and assistant Benko were cooperative. But out in the field, cooperation with local police stations was very difficult, particularly in the first couple of months in autumn in 1995 and spring-time 1996. There was virtually no cooperation at all. Another thing. The local population were afraid of the police and official organs, and we saw some documents, corroborate that when it was stated that they addressed with their concerns us and not the local police because they found it more acceptable. The third problem was -- my experience was that the top brass of the police did not receive data from the field immediately, and with Mr. Jarnjak and Mr. Benko, I spoke on several occasions, and I found out that they were misinformed. But after a while it would transpire that what data they had did not correspond to the state of affairs in the field. I attribute that to the poor organisation of the network of the institutions in the area that had been reintegrated into Croatia, and this meant that they most probably were not ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This was supposed to be my next question, Mr. Puhovski. You are aware, of course, that in the newly liberated territory, the Croatian authorities, and by this I mean the police and the judiciary, did not -- had not functioned for more than four years, and that they had to re-establish institutions of the system anew. Did this circumstance -- was recognised by the HHO in their reports and in their work?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had to recognise that because or activists confronted this situation daily, the situation where what was required of the authorities did not work or their functioning was negative towards Serb citizens. There were negative reaction towards them. In several months of the Autumn of 1995, we had 50 reports by people who claimed that they had been kicked out of police stations whenever they entered them to seek service, and when they introduced themselves and it could be concluded that they were Serbs from their names and family names. Some things could not progress further, but the problem was that it was claimed that everything was going okay, that the civilian authorities had taken control over the whole territory and that the whole territory had been reintegrated into the rest of the country, but for months after August 1995, this did not hold.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Without a doubt, it followed from the political will.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the very top of the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you talk about HHO activists a couple of days ago, you said something about their educational and professional profile or background. My question is: Among the HHO activists were there any people who had received any forensic or criminology training or background to recognise the situation out in the field?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I noticed, Mr. Puhovski, in the HHO's report - that's 65 ter 4674 - that very often, or as a rule, the Croatian term murder and killing is being used. Will you agree with me that that term has some legal connotations, which presumes an act of illegal termination of another person's life. And the accent is on "illegal"?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's no doubt about that. I answered that -- by Mr. Misetic yesterday. We use the term in a context which is not strictly legal discourse. I repeat, this report was not meant to be a report for a judicial institution. On the other hand, our understanding was that it went exclusively for people who were unlawfully killed. We did not deal with the loss of life during the military action. If that happened, we noted it as such, and in that case, certainly the word "murder" was not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But I presume you will agree with me, Professor Puhovski, that attribution of an unlawful act in the term "murder" by nature, would follow from a forensic process or some other process that would determine that this was so, and this is not something that would be prima vista -- be obvious to somebody who has no forensic training?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no dispute about that. We did not use the term in its legal sense, although if you take a look at the description carefully, in many cases, it corresponds to the technical or legal sense of the word, but this term, I repeat, was used in colloquial sense of the word and not strictly legal or technical sense of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your statement - and that would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your 2007 statement, which is P2316, MFI, in paragraph 10, you state that in mid-August 1995, you were briefly visiting Knin. Please tell me, was that your only visit to the Sector South that -- the area that the indictment deals with, that visit from mid-August 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement was in 2007. It says here in the transcript 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, could be my mistake or a typo.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited Knin only once in that period, as late as December 1995 for an hour or two, en route to somewhere else, and that was a period when we were engaged in -- in our first review of the area, and I was there for a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 of this statement, you say that your impression was that the police did not function properly, and you corroborated that by the fact that during your journeys, despite the presence of check-points in the territory, you were never stopped or questioned about what was -- what you were doing there. Professor Puhovski, had you been stopped and questioned, would this argumento a contrario mean that you were denied access to the area, which was the subject of the activities of the Croatian Helsinki Committee?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak as an expert. It seemed logical to me that it -- that each person passing there would have to be stopped and questioned. I had a letter explaining my mission there. It was in the glove compartment of my car, but I didn't reach for it even once because nobody asked me to show any kind of document. I encountered two policemen that I knew -- sorry, not policemen, soldiers. They just waved me through. I presumed that they recognised me. Both were my students. But this not seem professional control over territory, in my view, and these were not my journeys, just one single journey when I was passing through these places that this happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, without false modesty, then and now, you are a public figure and easily recognizable throughout Croatia. Is it not the case?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a public figure, but I was not popular, as it were. I was not focus of much public love. I was a bit hated, rather being loved by the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When, in your testimony, you discuss the facts indicated by the HHO's report, on several occasions you stated that that report was publicised, was sent to more than 300 addressees, and that you never received any refutals of the facts listed in that report. Do you think, Professor Puhovski, that absence of refutal may lead us to conclude that the facts contained in the report are credible?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a refutal by the minister of the interior and minister of the justice, but we proved them wrong. They claimed that one person from the list of casualties was alive. We did not find that they were right, but this prompted us to report -- to publish this report as a book, because two years had passed since its publication in the photocopied form, and we believed that those two years were ample time for all the reactions and feedback. Reactions were negative, but they were of an ideological nature. We were claimed to be Serbian mercenaries or the servants of an international Jewish conspiracy but nobody disputed the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at an example, much exploited at the time and still, and it concerns the incidents at the village of Grubori in P231 -- no, correction. 4674, on page 54 in the English version or page 56 in Croatian. What is discussed is that in the village of Grubori, a man, identified as Milos Grubor was shot behind his ear, and then I will quote part of that report. "Further on there was another house with a body on the floor in a room. We could not see who it was (Ivo Grubor born 1930, note PM)" I assume that stands for Petar Mrkalj. These are his initials.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: "The person talking to us said that he had brought the body during the afternoon while we were not there. When he turned the body over, the scene was horrible."

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm being shown the wrong page. In the e-court version, that would be page 54; and in the printed book, 53; English version 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So on the right-hand side of the screen, you have the right page. And the last sentence of this paragraph that I'm quoting is: "His throat was slashed in two." Furthermore it is stated: "Inhabitants of Grubori were killed by members of the special place, and for that reason until today the Republic of Croatia has not recognised this grave incident, has not investigated it, and has not provided answers to queries." In footnote number 48, there is reference to Alun Roberts, UN spokesperson in his interview to the Voice of America on the 11th of September, 1995, as your source. Mr. Puhovski, you are familiar with the incidents in the village of Grubori?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it known to you that because of the incident in the village of Grubori investigation has been initiated, that it's still ongoing, and that it has not been possible to identify the immediate perpetrators of this incident if it were a crime or criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed to us that the description of facts could correspond to a description of a criminal offence, but let the judiciary deal with that. We found about that when Mr. Bajic became state prosecutor general, 15 years after the fact. While we were preparing this report, we did not know that an investigation had been initiated because we were not given any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, let me acquaint with you one fact. Before this Trial Chamber a Mr. Zganger testified who, at the critical time, was a prosecutor in Sibenik. And it was within his jurisdiction that the investigation into this crime took place. He testified here and told us that an investigation was launched and that there were great difficulties. But we will get back to that later. Mr. Puhovski, look at this quotation which I think has to be attributed to Alun Roberts which says that he was presented when the inhabitants of the village of Grubori practically manipulated the dead body, turned it over, brought it out from the field into the house. Will you agree with me that this sort of conduct, to say the least, does not contribute to the establishment of facts and traces on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I think it is inaccurate to say that Mr. Roberts said that was present when people manipulated bodies. That is not what the quote says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
