utterances.text: If there is any doubt as to whether a quote is accurately summarized, you're invited, Mr. Mikulicic, as usual, to put exactly to the witness what you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I will quote the sentence which begins after the brackets and it says: "[Interpretation] The man who spoke with us told us that he had brought the body over in the course of the afternoon while we were not there. When he turned the body over, the scene was horrific. His throat had been splashed in two." Footnote 48 Alun Roberts, the UN spokesperson in Glas America -- Voice of America, on September 11, 1995. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but my conclusion is that the quotation is to be attributed to Mr. Alun Roberts. Would you agree with me, Mr. Puhovski?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt about the fact that this is something that Mr. Alun Roberts said. Let me go back to your earlier question. There were dozens of cases where individuals removed bodies to other locations. I heard audiotapes of people saying we placed the grandma on the bed to make it more comfortable for her. Of course, the grandma was dead. These were traditional customs. People were not used to having individuals and in violent death. People died of natural causes there. Throughout the war, the ethnic Serb population fully mistrusted the Croatian authorities. They did not expect anyone to show up and even less to show up and behave properly. I'm telling you that there were certain reasons there, there was idealogy there, but there were also some expectations on their part. Even those who knew something about it or who didn't know anything about it did not think it necessary to wait for the professionals, for the forensic officers to arrive, for the policemen to arrive. They simply wanted to put the -- sort things out, to get in touch with the relatives, and to get in touch with an institution. And most often that was the Helsinki Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puhovski. On the issue of the atmosphere that was pervasive in what was formerly in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and their attitude toward the Croatian authorities, this is something that we will get back to later. What is being described here is a very, very ugly fact which is that Mr. Jovo Grubor was killed and that he met his death by having had his throat cut in two. Similarly we were able to see a video, P2321, where the same statement was made by General Forand, who was commander of Sector South. This assertion that a man has had his throat cut found its way into the UN report and into the report of the HHO. And I will put the following question to you, Mr. Puhovski. Let us first see on our screens the dead body of Jovo Grubor. This is the photograph which is part of D1245. While we're waiting for the photograph to appear, let me tell you that Dr. Clark appeared here as an expert witness for the Prosecution, and he gave his expert findings here. He is a pathologist, who was present when a number of dead bodies that were exhumed in the area of Sector South were autopsied. He, himself, produced an autopsy report for Mr. Jovo Grubor. It is beyond doubt, he explained to the Trial Chamber here, that's at transcript page 14278, line 23, through to 14281, that a wound could that be observed on the neck of the body of Mr. Jovo Grubor does not originate from a wound -- from a -- from a knife.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... but from a bullet which is the source of the wound. Were you ever aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told your learned friend yesterday that on several occasions it so happened that the individuals would exaggerate the state in which the dead body was, and this was down to the shock and not much more. We did not have other possibilities than to publicise the information which was confirmed by two independent reports. This was information that was gathered by internationals who should have been professionals. It was not the case that a niece found the body of Mr. Jovo Grubor, and then she could be justified in exaggerating the condition in which the body was, which is something that we come across quite often. These were officers, and we had no reason to doubt what they said. This is all can I tell you in our defence. Now, when it comes to this story about it actually being a bullet rather than a knife, this is something that I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, let's be quite clear. You're not a position to state anything in your defence or in the defence of the Croatian Helsinki Committee. We're simply speaking about the facts here.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm trying to clarify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Similarly in your evidence so far you spoke of the issue of evacuation. I want to refer you to part of the report of the HHO, specifically page 15 of the Croatian version and 16 of the English version in e-court, and that's page 14 of the printed version. There, the statement of Nedelijka Draca is reported, who said that the information for evacuation was received by the population on the 2nd, and what is meant, of course, is the month of August, and the order to pack was received on the evening of the 3rd August. She goes on to say that on the 4th of August, in the morning, people started moving out in the direction of Donji Lapac. That's when the exodus started. You, the HHO activists, based on your fieldwork came to conclude that the evacuation of the Serb population was both organised an ordered. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, Mrs. Draca said that the people were notified by our leadership, and she is referring to the leadership of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The people were instilled great fear from the Croatian army. We had to avoid that. Those of us who were not fleeing hid very well to make sure that they did not find us. Otherwise, we would have to be running or else be killed by Serbs. They went from house to house to check if people were indeed leaving. Mr. Puhovski, this fact related to evacuation, was it an exception, or was it something that the HHO activists were able to ascertain in their fieldwork, were things that happened again and again?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were able to establish this in a number of locations in Sector South. As far as I know, in Sector North, there were certain areas where the decision to evacuate was sabotaged. Things unfolded differently there. Practically in all the cases known to us in Sector South, this is what things were like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, let me show you a part of the statement on this particular issue, which was given before this Tribunal in the case against Slobodan Milosevic by Djuro Matovina. That's at page 11.000, line 7, where the witness says -- and I will quote it in English. "[In English] Jovan Raskovic's speech was another speech of hatred. Inciting hatred between Serbs and Croats living in that area. Among other things he said, I remember one, he said that there is no future for Serbs in the independent state of Croatia, that another Ustasha government is in power, that if Serbs want autonomy and ask for it, they should have it. And he ended his speech with the words, Serb brothers, see you in Krajina. You will have no happiness in the Ustasha states." [Interpretation] This takes me back to the topic you broached a moment ago, Mr. Puhovski, which is the fear-inducing atmosphere, the aim being to instill fear in the Serbs from the Croatian authorities as an Ustasha authorities, which is something that had been present throughout the duration of the Serbian Krajina. Would you agree with this fact?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, indeed, the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Their Honours, I wish to refer you to the statements given by witnesses Sovilj, Sava Mirkovic, Jovan Vojnovic, and protected witness number 15. With regard to the atmosphere that was systematically being induced by the authorities of the so-called Republic of the Serbian Krajina, there exists another important witness statement of which I will read a paragraph to you, and then ask you to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the registrar's assistance. This is document 1D41-0214.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I hesitate to rise because I'm sure that foundation has already been laid, and, Mr. Mikulicic, I would like to remind of the procedure of putting other statements to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you have already questioned the witness about what you want to put to him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour. That is referring to the atmosphere which was prevailed in the Krajina state at those times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we are about to read now, Mr. Puhovski, is the statement by witness Slobodan Lazarovic. He gave a statement to the OTP investigators in 1999. I am at page 25 of the B/C/S version and page 26 of the English version. Allow me to read a paragraph to you. "In 1995, the life in Krajina became even harder for the local population. It seemed as if everyone had gone mad. People felt that they were imprisoned in that back of the beyond without any future. They decided to resolve any dispute they had with arms. A great many people participated in the killings of Croats in 1991 and later. Those who did not saw that the killings were being condoned, tolerated, by the official level. Once there were no Croats left there, violence spread among the Serbs themselves. The problem was further aggravated by the fact that the population was fully militarised. All the men aged between 18 and 65 were mobilized, but there were also volunteers who were only 16 years old, and those who were as old as 75. All of them were armed, and the law dictated that they should all wear their uniforms at all times, regardless of whether they were on duty or not." This portion of the statement, Mr. Puhovski, depicts the atmosphere and the situation in the Republic of Serbian Krajina prior to Operation Storm. Will you agree with me that inducing such an atmosphere among the population at large was one of the prerequisites for an evacuation to take place in the days preceding Operation Storm and which was to take place during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, are you aware of the fact - and this is something that the HHO's report speaks of - that the population which fled the Serbian Republic of Krajina fled to first Bosnia-Herzegovina and later on to Serbia. And in Serbia, which was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time, they were rechannelled to go to Kosovo, that parts of motorways were cordoned off in order to provide -- to channel them or funnel them through toward Kosovo. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that from newspaper articles and primarily from the writings of the institute for -- Fund for Humanitarian Law which primarily dealt with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Let me go back, while we still have the document on the screen, to the following passage of Mr. Lazarovic's statement, and that would be page 27 in the B/C/S version, or page 28 in the English version. He states: "Rumours were spread that the Ustashas would kill all of the civilians, and I am aware of some individuals who actually were tasked with going around to spread rumours to the effect that the Ustashas were slaughtering children. Under such circumstances no one is going to stay around to find out if the rumours are true or not. They are just going to leave. I myself concocted a story of civilians being massacred by the Muslims of the 5th Corps of the BH army in Topuska which got reported on CNN. There was no truth to the story at all." Professor Puhovski, did you actually learn that such false stories were spread to instill fear in the local population?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Propaganda was spread which was based on lies; but not, unfortunately, always in all cases based on lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, Slobodan Lazarovic on page 28 in the B/C/S and page 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Mikulicic you are referring to the Slobodan Lazarovic statement. Could you give us a clue as far as numbers are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is an ID, 410190. And I'm referring -- that's a translation. And I'm referring to the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this Chamber has no access to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it's on the screen now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the screen. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm now referring to the page 28 in the B/C/S version, and corresponding page in English version is - let me check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was primarily asking because the statement of Mr. Lazarovic has been used at earlier occasions, and I just couldn't find whether [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... It was never tendered and admitted because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That was the subject of our 92 bis motion which was denied, so we are now trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I just wanted to get clear again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Allow me another quote. Mr. Lazarovic talks with the OTP investigators and says: "Krajina Serbs in their majority had left before Croatian forces reached them. Most of them went to Bosnia or to Republika Srpska. At one border crossing into Republika Srpska, the authorities of the Republika Srpska closed that border crossing down and forced the refugees to pay 100 Deutschemarks for crossing over into their territory." Next paragraph: "Given the atmosphere of fear which had been rehashed over the preceding four years, and the tactic of instilling fear which was used after the Croatian offensive had started, very few Serbs were willing to stay in Topusko. People were -- people there were in a state of mass panic, and a number of Serbs shot each other in dispute." On the next page, and I will finish quoting Mr. Lazarovic. "However, when we reached Serbia we were treated as criminals. We were all frisked, our weapons were taken away, and only then were we allowed to continue on your way. But when we entered Serbia we saw that the police had blocked all exits from the motorway. They did so in an attempt to force the refugees to continue towards Kosovo." Professor Puhovski, my question is, following from your testimony. Is it correct that the evacuation plan that had been prepared in the Republic of Serbian Krajina was a continuation of a plan for the refugee citizens of Serb ethnicity to be settled in Kosovo, as a counterweight to the Albanian population of the then Serbian province of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can repeat what I said in public about that, there were two reasons on the part of the Serbian leadership or the then Yugoslav leadership, one was to dismerge the predominantly positive image of Croatia as a victim of aggression. And the second was to obtain some ethnic Serb population to change the ethnic composition of the province of Kosovo, Koseva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... into the evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. The Prosecution has not had a chance to test this evidence in these proceedings, so, therefore, at this stage we would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But this is an official OTP document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes. But it was taken for a different proceedings, and we -- we have even statements taken perhaps for the purpose of these proceedings have been MFI if the witness has not appeared. We strongly object to the admission of this evidence without the evidence of the witness being heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, first of all, you have read a part of a statement to the witness and then you asked him something which was -- well, to some extent related to it, so this witness testified about his knowledge. Now, under what Rule would you like to have the statement to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As a corroborative statement to the testifying of present witness, Mr. Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if this is a statement which is prepared for the purposes of the proceedings before this Tribunal, then, of course, if you would have it tendered under Rule 92 bis, that is, without cross-examination, then you know what the requirements are, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the Chamber, an application is usually made, and then the Chamber will decide whether the witness should be called for cross-examination, yes or no. We have no attestation from this witness. So, therefore, it looks as if the requirements of Rule 92 bis are not met. And I just inquired, and Mr. Misetic told me, yes, we wanted to have it admitted under Rule 92 bis, and the Chamber denied that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was a different situation at that time. But really I don't want to have an another argument on it. We will try to prepare a motion on it, and then we could have a Trial Chamber's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will have to dive again into the circumstances which led us at that time to decide as we did. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, there is another matter, the timing. Apparently, you want to have the witness to testify before this Chamber on behalf of the Defence. Now, we have had situations where statements were taken by the Defence during the Prosecution's case, and at some moments there was no disagreement on how to proceed with that. But, of course, the introduction of a 92 bis or a 92 ter at this stage of te proceedings requested by the Defence is ... but I will first have to look again into the earlier decision on the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Puhovski, I would like to ask you to comment, and while we're waiting for the document to appear, which is 3D00-0212, in your testimony and in your statement you said that while the report is being prepared you were not aware that the Croatian authorities were undertaken investigations into incidents that may indicate a commission of a criminal offence. Did you learn later how many cases there were concerning crimes that were committed during or after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received information only when Mr. Bajic became state prosecutor general, and they -- that's information indicated in a large number of cases, but also -- it is indicated that the qualifications of the criminal offence was not war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What we see on the screen is a letter by the Croatian public Prosecutor's office to a law firm Mikulicic, Loncaric, Bahun, Topic on criminal offences committed during and after Operation Storm. If we look at page 3 of this document. If you do so, we can see a summary of the number of criminal offences, the number of proceedings, almost 4.000 criminal offences. Then the document discusses how many criminal reports been rejected, how many investigations were ongoing during the preparation of that document, how many charges or indictments were brought. On the next page we have a table stating that almost 2.000 judgements were handed down, out of which 1.500 convictions and 180 acquittals. Furthermore, it is discussed what were the qualifications of those criminal offences. We can see it is two pages down the road, criminal offences of murder, robbery, rape, and causing fire. Those figures are important, Mr. Puhovski. Did the Croatian Helsinki Committee ever supplement its report on Operation Storm with the data that could be provided by the state prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because, at the movement when this was published, in 2001, they could have given that information, but they did not. And I repeat that I received this information a couple of years later, when this book had only been published.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is no objection, then we should continue. But it is a bit unclear. I was waiting for the translation where Ms. Frolich started to say something. She more or less interrupted the answer of the witness. No objection, not against the question, not against anything. Then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just waiting for the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's unclear to me. On the -- that's why I'm reading the transcript. I do not see any tendering on the transcript at this moment. But you tendered this letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No. I tendered the whole document, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I mean the one -- let me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But just to understand fully the document. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I may of any assistance. It's a ten-page document which contains a cover letter from the Croatian attorney office, and as an attachment, the data referring to the crimes committed within or after the Operation Storm. So it's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The letter is from January 2006. By the way, I've got a 11-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe in English. I counted the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could be a difference. Now, are you tendering this document at this moment. Because I think the witness said - let me check that as well. Got a problem with my system. If you forgive me for one second, Mr. Mikulicic, I have to get the right transcript on my ... Yes. You asked -- first of all, you told the witness that the figures are important, that apparently is your opinion about the importance. Now, you put to the witness an overview of numbers which you received in 2006. The only thing you did is you asked witness whether he considered these figures when the report was written. He said, no, because it wasn't there at that time. Now, what -- how does the chamber have to understand tendering this document for the truth of its content or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, absolutely. But this document was not prepared in 2006. This document was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it was sent to you in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And let's then have a closer look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There is only the portion of a more voluminous document, which is already, I believe, in possession of the Office of the Prosecutor of this fine Tribunal. This is it only a portion of this huge document which is dealing with the criminal offences connected with Bljesak and Oluja operations. So it shows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, but what is in the hands of the Prosection is not our concern, Mr. Mikulicic. Our concern is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Our concern is what we are supposed to do with this information, because the witness just said, I wasn't aware of it. Well, now, if we would accept every document where a witness comes and says, I'm not aware of that, to have it then tendered for the truth of the content, that, of course, would be -- well, I would give, I would say, great opportunities to all parties to get everything into evidence. They wish to have in evidence without any -- so, therefore, I'm just inquiring with you the background of this [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, with all due respect, Your Honour, if I may of assistance, the witness said in his testimony that he was not aware that the Croatian authorities has been conducted some investigations on or procedures before the judicial system in Croatia concerning to the crimes committed during or after the Operation Storm. This document officially delivered by the Croatian attorney office, general attorney office, has established the fact that there has been a lot of these investigations, so that the part of the witness's testimony that he isn't aware is not necessary the fact that we have to combine with -- that there was no such investigation and procedures. So that was my point, just the point of fact that the Chamber could be aware of the numerous procedures that has been undertaken concerning the crimes committed during or after the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's exactly now the point I want to -- I can follow you to the extent that this document contradicts apparently what the witness said. Now, so either of them must be not accurate. Now, if you say, This is the reflection of what is the real truth and, therefore, please accept on the basis of this document, that the witness is not telling us what happened, but that this document tells us what happened, leaving apart a third possibility that neither the witness nor the document tells us what happened. But to say that this is for the accuracy of this document and, of course, I tend to agree with you that these figures are important, to introduce this through this witness may ask for some further consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we may ask the witness whether he is now aware of those proceedings that has been -- that has been introduced after the -- after the Operation Storm has finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether or not that is -- we could ask him. Mr. Puhovski, could you tell us, did you become aware of a large number of prosecutions in relation to offences committed during Operation Storm, after you had written the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already said, I received from Mr. Mladen Bajic, the state prosecutor general, roughly a similar document, and I have no reason to doubt the truthfulness of it. At the time of the drafting and publishing of the report, none of it was information known to either us or the public at large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you -- and you said you have no reasons to doubt the figures given. It's not in contradiction with what you learned from other sources. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat. To my knowledge, the information contained therein is accurate. We were not either primarily or secondarily engaged in trying to find out who was responsible. We wanted to ascertain the facts. We were not able to know anything about these proceedings because they were not referred to in public, save for two or three exceptions, like the Varivode case, and especially not in this summarily way, not until Mr. Mladen Bajic assumed the position of the state prosecutor general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to also have a look at the document so that I know what exactly, apart from the quoted portions, we find in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document being tendered for the truth of its content. Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, there are no objections to the admissibility, but I would just like to draw the Chamber's attention to the -- to the kinds of statistics that are put in this report as well as to the fact that it listed crimes committed linked to the Flash and Storm military operations. It doesn't break down any further recording, for example, exactly what types of proceedings were initiated for Operation Storm, as opposed to Operation Flash, against whom, what type of perpetrator, what ethnicity of perpetrator and victim, et cetera. When these proceedings were initiated all these are relevant factors to be taken into consideration by the Chamber when deciding what weight to attach to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that could be part of some other document, but as it concerns to this one, I'm only referring to the figures that has been put down by the Attorney General of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will have a look at. If it could be marked for identification for the time being, then the Chamber will decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit D1331, marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Puhovski, your line of profession strictly speaking is not sociology, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a professor of philosophy, social -- political sciences and social philosophy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But I do presume that in your line of work you had to deal with certain sociological issues, at least that is how you presented it during your evidence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the book by professor Ozren Zunec? He is a professor at the Faculty of Philosophy in Zagreb. He refers to a sociological theory. The book is called "The Bare Living." And the theory is that of collective violence.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When confronted with violence which was evidently present in the wake of Operation Storm, and where evidently a number of criminal offences was committed, Professor Zunec attempted to explain this by employing the theory of collective violence. He said that in certain situations such violence arises as a universal phenomenon. He draws a parallel with the riots in Los Angeles in 1992 where 50.000 people were involved, and where more than 50 persons were killed. He draws a parallel with Kosovo, where, after the intervention of the NATO alliance in 2004, riots erupted where many homes were burned, people killed, many Serbs fled. He also cites the example of France, in 2005, et cetera. Can you tell us what you know of this theory of collective violence and if, in your view, it can be somehow applied to the events in the aftermath of Operation Storm, in the newly liberated areas.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the strictly technical term, the theory of collective violence is a subheading of the theory of collective action, although we shouldn't go into great detail now. Recently it has been developed as a theoretical or philosophical approach at defining violence which is connected with the ideological apparata of the state. In other words, the violence which the state or other bodies, but most likely the state induces by creating collective identity which should somehow override individual identity. In other words, to create an atmosphere in which every individual in any times of crisis would automatically side with the collective, regardless of the person's own ideological or political or professional affinities. It is connected to the theory of ethnic nationalism which was developed mostly by some of the British experts and which was used to interpret the events in Northern Ireland. It seems to me that the interpretation advanced by Colleague Zunec, in connection with the local Croatian circumstances, is quite correct, and it does move within the realm of the theory itself and of the reality in Croatia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puhovski. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. It will depend on how many questions you would have, whether we proceed before the break, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I only have a few questions for the witness. I believe we can finish before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, in paragraph 15 of your 2009 statement you mentioned that initially in 1995 and 1996 there was no intent to publish information collected during your fact-finding missions. I'm asking you this: Whose idea was to initiate this project of these fact-finding missions and collection of information in the first place.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Originally this was the proposal by Mr. Petar Mrkalj, on his return from the first mission of the International Helsinki Federation. Since, at the time, I was the only member of the committee present in Zagreb, I immediately agreed with the suggestion, and, in September of 1995, or in October, I can't remember correctly, when we had enough people for the Plenary session, the Plenary decided that we should embark on the fact-finding mission since it became quite evident at the time that the public was being served one-sided information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Mrkalj was influenced by any external factors or external pressure to go and investigate the alleged incidents in the Krajina region?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally speaking, as deputy president, I dispatched Mr. Mrkalj to Knin, together with representatives of the IHF, so that could have been some sort of pressure. But he could have been influenced by some members of the IHF team. At the time, practically no one outside of the close circle of people knew what was going on, and there could have been no pressure to speak of, since the topic in relation to which pressure was supposed to be exerted was not known to the public. Once the HHO decided as its Plenary that we should be dealing this, we needed further two months to raise funds for that mission, which was initially primarily coming from the Soros Foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: At the time of the fact-finding missions, were you given any external directions on how to report and what to put emphasis on?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this issue solely with representatives of the United Nations in Croatia, with the people from the International Helsinki Committee, and with the colleagues from Serbia, who were engaged in similar activities in the human rights committee or the fund for humanitarian law. At the time these were practically the only individuals outside of Croatia whom we engaged experience with and discussed work methodology.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: And, lastly, when exactly did you obtain the funding to publish the report, if you could say?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the publication of the report in the form of the book, I can't tell that, because this transpired at the time when I was not on the committee. In late 1999, when the photocopied version was published, I can tell that when I became president in late 2000, the documentation relevant to the book, this is something that I was privy to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, I don't know whether you are familiar with the issue I will raise in my question, but do you know how houses were defined in the 1991 census? Because what we have seen here apparently is that there are reports about many more houses observed for the purposes of whether they were damaged or not; and, at the same time, we see in the 1991 census that not that number of houses apparently have been establish to exist in 1991. Are you aware of how houses were defined in the 1991 census? If they were defined as such.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only give you an indirect answer. I know for a fact that in the 1981 census, the following formulation was used: Family house and the attendant farm buildings or outbuildings. As far as I know, that was the premise from which the census was made in 1981 because at the time I was involved in the process to a certain degree. I don't know how this was done in 1991. It is quite possible that the same methodology was applied. Let me only note that the census was made at the time when Yugoslavia was already breaking up, and probably whatever methodology was used, it was not applied properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if you say, "family houses and the attendant farm buildings or outbuildings," I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am familiar myself with a situation where, for example, in the countryside a family is living and when the parents grow older, either the parents move out and live on the same yard, let's say, within a distance of anything between 10 and 50 metres, create their own house; or that the children move out of the parental house and live, although nearby, a similar distance, and don't criticise me for whether it should be 50, 70 metres, but just close to the parents. Under the 1981 census such a situation where two generations would live in the same -- more or less on the same farm yard, to say so, would that be one house or to houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer depends on how many house numbers they were allocated. In the countryside they would have old numbering systems. They wouldn't have individual house numbers, but the entire village would have a number. Now, if there was one house number that referred to a given yard, in a given village, then that was normally considered to be one household. This is something that I know from the 1981 census, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And whether that was still was valid in 1991, you just don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. That was my question to you. Any need for further questions? Then, Mr. Puhovski, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for not only for coming to The Hague and for answering the questions put to you by the Bench and by the parties but also for your patience and even for re-scheduling your return home, and I hope that everything with your return this afternoon goes well. Thank you. Would you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, we have been advised by the Ms. Frolich that the OTP has no objection to our bar table for this witness so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the registrar is invited to provisionally assign numbers to them so that the Chamber can decide on admission. The Chamber has decided and puts on the record that the application for videolink for Witness 82 is granted. Reasons to follow, but it is important that preparations can start for the videolink. I have one question for you, Mr. Mikulicic, in relation to the data that was sent to you in February 2006. The cover letter says something about reports of -- of prosecutors. Because from the cover letter I take it that one of your specific questions was, Have there been cases in proceedings in cases of persons who, according to the indictment, were killed. So that is a far more individualized question than we see from this answer. Now, in the letter, I read that what is sent to you is the report submitted to the government and to the president of Croatia on the numbers, and it's added the records are fragmentary because of fully defined methodology of recording was never agreed on, and it says we are forwarding both or data and the from other sources in the hope that you will find this useful for the proceedings. And then a warning follows that the data are cumulative and that the breakdown would require insight in all the documents. Then it says in your letter, you included the list of persons who were killed, as alleged in the amended indictment, and that your request to be provided with data you could use to establish a collection. Then it says that this list was forwarded to all public prosecutors, and that you are sent copies of the reports submitted by them. Now, the document you seek to tender into evidence, that's a cover letter and a report, what is attached to the cover letter? Is that all the information you received in the response to your request? Or have you made a selection? For example, one of the things that might be interesting is to see how the prosecutor's report on proceedings in cases where the alleged victim appears in the indictment. That might be quite interesting information. Have you received that? Have you made a selection on what you attached to this letter? Or is it everything you received?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, there are a lot of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to answer them. First, what is attached to this cover letter is only part of the documents that I have received from the attorney general's office. Second, I only partially received the answer to my questions, whether it refers to the connection with a annexed list of the murdered victims during and after the operation Storm. This was -- this type of arrangement has never been completed, not today. So I just, for the purposes of that witness, compose the document of 10 or 11 pages, whatever version he is counting on and try to establish the fact that there was a huge number of the criminal proceedings carrying on after the Operation Storm. That was my whole purpose, just to inform the Chamber that the Croatian government has been taking the steps, trying to prosecute the alleged perpetrators of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, it's not limited to Storm and aftermath, or is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the second page of the document, then it is written that these are the crimes committed in connections with the operation Bljesak and Oluja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is not limited --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is not limited.

utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President, I don't believe that there are in fact actual portions of these -- these exhibits are portions of P2241. There may that be that the contents are nearly identical. And I should have to check if they are in such a way similar so that we do not have to tender them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very practical. There are no objections. We're not going to wait for P2241. And there being no objections, P2205 is admitted into evidence. P2206, there are no objections and is, therefore, also is admitted into evidence. P2207 is the same as we discussed before; part of 2241. Although the Prosecution does not yet agree to that, but it will be -- it is admitted into evidence. P2208, there are no objections, is admitted into evidence. P2209. I think this document was used by the Defence in cross, and there was an issue about whether the one document was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P2209 is a part of P1013. And I think there was an issue about whether it was complete or not. The Chamber has carefully checked, and it seems to be in there completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, we would like to vacate this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P2209 is vacated. Then the next one is one of a long list, that's P2210, which is not on the 65 ter list. I think we earlier asked the Prosecution to make an application for any document not appearing yet on the 65 ter list to have it admitted to that list before we can decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It was suggested to us, and I believe that if we -- I can make an oral application at this time for all the outstanding documents that were -- that were to be admitted to the 65 ter list that were present on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are they all not on the 65 ter list for the same reason? Or do we get a variety of reasons why they should now be admitted, where they earlier were not on that list? Because if we get to a series of reasons why, then, of course, it's -- if you say, This is all material that we received two weeks ago, that's clear. Then the Defence would now how to answer. utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: That would be more applicable to this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will not further deal with any of the -- then I just do a few more, but then we have to stop. utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Just a comment. What I have is that P2221 and P2222 were in fact parts of larger 65 ters. P2221 was part of 65 ter 3918, and P2222 is in fact duplicate of 65 ter 1869. Therefore, I don't believe there's reason to add them to -- because they're already on 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll verify that. We have to stop for the time being. Unfortunately, we were not able to finish the whole list, but we made at least some progress.
